title: The Spiral, the Zeros, and the Primes

chapters.title: A Machine for Primes
chapters.subtitle: The Riemann zeta function, drawn in three dimensions

lines.text: This is the Riemann zeta function, drawn as a spiral that climbs a line through the complex plane.
Every time the spiral closes on the origin, a zero is born, and that zero becomes a wave.
Add enough of those waves together and a staircase appears, stepping up at every prime number.
In the next few minutes we will build this picture from scratch, find the hidden axis, and see what a 2026 result changes.

chapters.title: Building the Spiral
chapters.subtitle: One arrow per term of the zeta series

lines.text: Zeta starts as an infinite sum: one, plus one over two to the s, plus one over three to the s, and so on forever.
Each term is an arrow. Its length shrinks like one over the square root of n, because the real part of s is one half.
And each arrow is rotated by the imaginary part of s, by an angle of t times the log of n. The arrows chain head to tail.
But here is the catch. On the critical line the plain sum never converges. Sixteen arrows, or a thousand, land nowhere in particular.
The fix is Euler and Maclaurin's. The missing tail of the sum is almost exactly an integral, and we can draw that integral as one more arrow.
Add it, plus a few tiny Bernoulli corrections, and the chain lands on the true value of zeta to thirteen decimal places.
lines.footnote: ζ(s) = Σ n^-s (n < N)  +  N^(1-s)/(s-1)  +  N^-s/2  +  Bernoulli terms      N ≈ t/2 + 4

lines.text: That orange arrow is the difference between a pretty picture and an exact one. Now the spiral really does predict the zeros.
Here is the part that confuses everyone, including me. There are two complex planes in this picture, not one.
The input, s, lives on the glowing panel to the left. Its real part runs left to right, from zero to one.
Its imaginary part, t, runs straight up. So the vertical direction of this whole scene is the imaginary axis of the input.
We only feed zeta points with real part one half, so the input crawls up the critical line in the middle of the strip.
The output is a second complex number, drawn flat. Real part to the right, imaginary part toward the back.
So the spiral lives in the output plane, floating at the height of its input. Climb the input axis and the spiral redraws itself.
A zero is simply an input whose output lands on the origin: the spiral closes, and we drop a yellow marker on the vertical axis.

chapters.title: Hunting Zeros
chapters.subtitle: Hardy's Z function makes the hunt visible

lines.text: Riemann's Z function makes the hunt visible. It is zeta rotated to be real, so it just wiggles left and right of the critical line.
Every time the wiggle crosses the line, zeta is exactly zero. The first crossing is at t equals fourteen point one three four seven.
Then twenty one point zero two, twenty five point zero one, thirty point four two. The zeros keep coming, irregular but never missing.
Every one of the ten thousand zeros we loaded sits precisely on the line. Nobody has ever found one anywhere else.
lines.footnote: zeros from the LMFDB table · Assets/Resources/zetazeros.txt

lines.text: Now the magic. Each zero, gamma, becomes a wave in x: the cosine of gamma times the log of x.
One wave says nothing. But stack the waves from many zeros and they interfere, cancelling almost everywhere.
Where they do not cancel, they spike. And they spike exactly at the primes and their powers: two, three, four, five, seven, eight, nine, eleven.
Riemann's explicit formula turns that chorus into a staircase. Start with the line psi equals x, then subtract four root x times a weighted wave for every zero.
The weights, cosine plus two gamma sine over one plus four gamma squared, come from dividing x to the rho by rho. Nothing is fudged.
lines.footnote: ψ(x) = x − Σ_ρ x^ρ/ρ − ln 2π − ½ ln(1 − x^-2)        ρ = ½ ± iγ

lines.text: With a few hundred zeros the staircase sharpens and the red markers find the primes on their own: two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen.
The zeros of zeta and the primes are the same information, written in two languages. The spiral is the translator.

chapters.title: Why One Half Matters
chapters.subtitle: The real part sets the size of every wave

lines.text: Why does everyone care that the zeros sit at real part one half? Because the real part sets the size of each wave.
A zero at real part beta adds a wave of height x to the beta. At one half, that is the square root of x, the smallest wobble possible.
Suppose a rogue zero existed at real part zero point nine. Its wave would grow like x to the zero point nine, and the staircase would be wrecked.
lines.footnote: red: the staircase if the first zero were moved from ½ + 14.13i to 0.9 + 14.13i (hypothetical)

lines.text: The Riemann Hypothesis says no such rogue exists. The error in counting primes is essentially as small as it can be: about the square root of x, for every x.
On October sixth, 2026, OpenAI released an AI generated proof of what it calls the quasi Riemann hypothesis.
lines.footnote: openai/math · family 003 · manuscript dated Sept 30, 2026 · released Oct 6, 2026

lines.text: The claim: the zeta function, and every Dirichlet L function, has no zeros with real part greater than seven eighths.
By the functional equation that also clears everything below one eighth. The shaded bands are now off limits.
Before this, the known zero free region was a sliver hugging real part one, shrinking as t grows. A fixed wall at seven eighths is new territory.
The proof goes through cubic theta functions and Hecke L functions over Q adjoined root negative three, then transfers to zeta. A companion paper reaches eleven twelfths by a different route.
The core theorem was formalized in Lean and re checked by an independent kernel. Human peer review is still in progress, so treat it as a strong claim, not settled fact.
lines.footnote: Lean statement: riemannZeta s ≠ 0 for 7/8 < Re s · axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound · not yet peer reviewed

lines.text: For the staircase it means every rogue wave is at most x to the seven eighths. For this picture it means the yellow markers can only hide in the narrow unshaded band.
The gap from seven eighths down to one half is where the Riemann Hypothesis still lives. Commentators expect the method to stall near three quarters. A new idea is needed.
So this is the state of play. Ten thousand zeros on the line, a spiral that lands on every one of them, and a wall at seven eighths.
Prove the wall is at one half and the primes are finally tamed. Until then, watch the spiral climb.
